conditions.action: For a bee or wasp sting: scrape the sting out sideways (don't squeeze it), put on a cold pack, and use an antihistamine and simple pain relief for the swelling and itch. Most reactions are local and settle in a day or two.
conditions.red: Swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, trouble breathing, widespread hives, dizziness or collapse after a sting is a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) — use an adrenaline pen if you have one and call emergency services.

conditions.name: Unsettled / crying child
conditions.action: A baby or child who won't settle often has a simple cause — hunger, wind, a dirty nappy, teething, or being too hot or cold — but it can also be an infection. Check for fever, how they're feeding, and wet nappies, and comfort them. If they stay inconsolable, feed poorly, or you're worried, have them seen.
conditions.red: A high fever, a rash that doesn't fade when pressed, a bulging soft spot on the head, a stiff neck, fast or laboured breathing, floppiness, or far fewer wet nappies — get urgent medical help.

conditions.name: Sore / wound that won't heal
conditions.action: A sore or wound that hasn't healed in a few weeks should be checked. Causes include infection, poor circulation or diabetes, constant pressure, or less often a skin cancer. Keep it clean and covered, relieve pressure on it, and see a clinician to find and treat the cause.
conditions.red: Spreading redness, pus or a bad smell, fever, blackening skin, or a non-healing sore in someone with diabetes or poor circulation — get seen promptly.

conditions.name: Erection difficulty
conditions.action: Trouble getting or keeping an erection is common and usually treatable. Stress, tiredness, alcohol, low mood and some medicines are frequent causes — but it can also be an early sign of heart/blood-vessel disease or diabetes, so a check-up (blood pressure, blood sugar, review of medicines) is worthwhile. A clinician can talk through causes and treatment options.
conditions.red: New erection trouble together with chest pain or breathlessness when active — get your heart checked promptly.

conditions.name: Vaginal thrush (yeast infection)
conditions.action: Thick white 'cottage-cheese' discharge with itching and soreness (and little smell) is usually thrush — a common yeast overgrowth, not an STI. It's treated with an antifungal pessary/cream or a single oral capsule from a pharmacy; avoid soaps/douches on the area and wear cotton underwear. See a clinician if it's the first time, keeps coming back (4+ times a year), you're pregnant, or it doesn't settle in a week.
conditions.red: Fever, lower-belly or pelvic pain, or feeling unwell — see a clinician, as that points beyond simple thrush.

conditions.name: Bacterial vaginosis
conditions.action: Thin greyish-white discharge with a fishy smell (often stronger after sex) and little itching is typically bacterial vaginosis — an imbalance of normal bacteria, not usually an STI. It's treated with antibiotics (metronidazole) from a clinician; avoid douching and scented products. It can clear on its own but is worth treating, especially in pregnancy.
conditions.red: Pelvic pain, fever, or discharge after a new partner with other symptoms — get checked, including for STIs.

conditions.name: Possible sexually transmitted infection
conditions.action: Yellow or green (sometimes frothy) discharge — especially with pelvic pain, pain passing urine, bleeding between periods or after sex, or a recent new partner — can mean an STI such as chlamydia, gonorrhoea or trichomonas. Get tested at a sexual-health or primary-care clinic; these are treatable with antibiotics, and partners should be treated too. Testing is confidential.
conditions.red: Fever, severe lower-belly pain, or feeling very unwell can mean the infection has spread (pelvic inflammatory disease) — seek care promptly.

conditions.name: Late or missed period
conditions.action: A late or missed period has many causes. If there's any chance of pregnancy, do a home urine test — most are accurate from the first day of a missed period (repeat in a week if negative but still no period). Other common causes are stress, big weight change or exercise, illness, coming off contraception, thyroid problems, PCOS, or approaching menopause. If periods are often irregular, you're not pregnant and it keeps happening, see a clinician to look into why.
conditions.red: A positive test with one-sided pelvic pain, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness or bleeding can be an ectopic pregnancy — seek emergency care. Also see someone if you could be pregnant and have heavy bleeding or severe pain.

conditions.name: Self-harm — support available
conditions.action: Thank you for telling me — that takes courage, and you deserve support. You don't have to manage this alone. Consider reaching out to someone you trust or a crisis line: in the US and Canada call or text 988; in the UK call 111 or Samaritans on 116 123. If any wound is deep, won't stop bleeding, or you've hurt yourself more than you meant to, get medical care now. A GP or mental-health service can help you find longer-term support.
conditions.red: If you are thinking about ending your life, or a wound is serious (deep, heavy bleeding, or over a joint/artery), contact emergency services now.

conditions.name: Disordered eating — support available
conditions.action: What you're describing with food and eating can be really hard, and support helps — you deserve it. Please consider talking to a GP or a specialist service; in the US the National Alliance for Eating Disorders helpline (1-866-662-1235) can guide you, and your doctor can refer you to care. These difficulties are common and treatable, and reaching out early makes recovery easier.
conditions.red: Fainting, chest pain, a very low or irregular heartbeat, or vomiting blood need urgent medical care.

conditions.name: Feeling detached / unreal (dissociation)
conditions.action: Feeling detached from yourself or like the world isn't real (dissociation) is often linked to stress, anxiety, trauma, poor sleep or panic, and usually eases as those are addressed. Grounding techniques (naming things you can see/hear/touch, slow breathing) can help in the moment. If it's frequent, distressing, or affecting daily life, a GP or mental-health professional can help find the cause and support you.
conditions.red: New confusion, slurred speech, weakness, or detachment after a head injury or with a very fast/irregular heartbeat needs urgent assessment.

conditions.name: Bleeding / sore gums (gingivitis)
conditions.action: Gums that bleed when brushing are usually gum inflammation (gingivitis) from plaque. Brush gently twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, clean between teeth daily, and see a dentist/hygienist — it's reversible with good cleaning. Persistent bleeding can also relate to pregnancy, some medicines, or (rarely) a bleeding/blood disorder.
conditions.red: Gums bleeding a lot or spontaneously, with easy bruising or bleeding elsewhere, should be checked promptly.

conditions.name: Blood clot in the lung (pulmonary embolism) — consider
conditions.action: A clot from the leg can travel to the lungs. Sudden breathlessness or chest pain with a swollen, tender calf needs emergency care now — call your local emergency number.
conditions.red: sudden breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood, collapse

conditions.name: Cauda equina (spinal emergency) — consider
conditions.action: Back pain with numbness between the legs, trouble passing or controlling urine, or new leg weakness can mean the nerves at the base of the spine are being crushed. This is an emergency — being seen within hours protects against lasting damage. Go now.
conditions.red: saddle numbness, bladder/bowel changes, leg weakness

conditions.name: Twisted testicle (torsion) — consider
conditions.action: A sudden painful, often swollen testicle — sometimes felt as lower belly pain with nausea or vomiting, especially in boys and young men — can be a torsion. The testicle can only be saved if treated within hours. Go to emergency care now.
conditions.red: sudden testicle pain, swelling, nausea/vomiting

conditions.name: Deep spreading skin infection (necrotising fasciitis) — consider
conditions.action: Pain much worse than the injury looks, spreading redness, and feeling very unwell can mean a deep infection that destroys tissue quickly. Do not wait — go to emergency care now.
conditions.red: pain out of proportion, spreading redness, fever, feeling very unwell

conditions.name: Multiple sclerosis (consider)
conditions.action: Nerve symptoms that come and go over weeks — numbness, weakness, or eye problems that move around — can have many causes, including MS. A neurologist can assess this with an examination and usually an MRI.
conditions.red: sudden weakness or numbness on one side, slurred speech, or loss of vision (seek emergency care — could be a stroke)

conditions.name: Encephalitis (brain inflammation) — consider
conditions.action: Fever or headache with new confusion, strange behaviour, or a fit can mean inflammation of the brain. This is an emergency — call your local emergency number now.
conditions.red: drowsiness, fits, weakness, or a stiff neck with fever

conditions.name: Peripheral neuropathy (nerve damage)
conditions.action: Tingling, numbness or burning in both hands and feet can come from nerve damage — common causes include diabetes, low B12 and some medicines. Your GP can test for a cause.
conditions.red: rapidly spreading weakness or numbness moving up the limbs (seek urgent care — could be Guillain-Barré)

conditions.name: Nerve-related burning or itch (neuropathic)
conditions.action: A long-standing burning or 'sunburn-like' feeling in one spot — especially if it later went numb, if you keep scratching the same place, or if a 'nerve medicine' was prescribed before — often comes from an irritated or damaged nerve (neuropathic pain or itch) rather than a skin burn or infection. Common local causes include a nerve pinched near the spine and nerve irritation left after shingles. This is not an emergency, but it's worth seeing your doctor: they can examine the area and the nerves, look for a cause, and discuss options such as nerve-targeted treatments or a referral to a neurologist or dermatologist. Because scratching can damage numb skin without you feeling it, protecting the area and keeping the skin moisturised helps.
conditions.red: a new band of blistering rash (possible shingles), new weakness, loss of bladder or bowel control, or a skin spot that is changing in size, colour or shape — see a clinician promptly.

conditions.name: Essential tremor
conditions.action: A shake that shows up when you use your hands (reaching, holding a cup) is often a benign 'essential' tremor, especially if it runs in the family. A clinician can tell it apart from other causes.
conditions.red: a tremor at rest with stiffness and slowness (worth checking for Parkinson's), or sudden new tremor with other symptoms

conditions.name: Labyrinthitis / vestibular neuritis
conditions.action: Severe spinning dizziness, often after a cold, with nausea and unsteadiness, can be inflammation of the balance nerve. It usually settles over days to weeks; a clinician can confirm and rule out other causes.
conditions.red: spinning with slurred speech, weakness, a bad headache, or deafness (seek urgent care)

conditions.name: Ménière's disease (consider)
conditions.action: Attacks of spinning dizziness with ringing, fullness and fluctuating hearing in one ear can be Ménière's. An ENT specialist can assess and manage it.
conditions.red: sudden permanent hearing loss, or spinning with neurological symptoms

conditions.name: Restless legs syndrome
conditions.action: An urge to move the legs with a creepy-crawly feeling, worse in the evening and relieved by moving, is restless legs syndrome. Checking iron levels and reviewing medicines often helps.
conditions.red: new one-sided leg weakness or numbness (different problem — get checked)

conditions.name: Collapsed lung (pneumothorax) — consider
conditions.action: Sudden sharp one-sided chest pain with breathlessness can be a collapsed lung, especially in tall slim young people or after chest injury. Seek emergency care now.
conditions.red: severe breathlessness, blue lips, or faintness

conditions.name: Whooping cough (pertussis) — consider
conditions.action: Severe coughing fits — sometimes ending in a 'whoop', vomiting, or struggling to breathe between coughs — can be whooping cough. See a clinician; it is treatable and infectious, and dangerous for babies.
conditions.red: a baby who goes blue, stops breathing, or struggles to feed (emergency)

conditions.name: Epiglottitis (airway emergency) — consider
conditions.action: A severe sore throat with drooling, a muffled voice, and sitting forward to breathe can be a swelling that blocks the airway. This is an emergency — call your local emergency number now and keep the person calm and upright.
conditions.red: noisy breathing, drooling, or struggling to breathe

conditions.name: Obstructive sleep apnoea
conditions.action: Loud snoring with pauses in breathing, gasping awake, and daytime exhaustion can be sleep apnoea. A sleep study can confirm it, and treatment makes a big difference to energy and heart health.
conditions.red: falling asleep while driving (stop driving and seek urgent advice)

conditions.name: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT)
conditions.action: A sudden, very fast heartbeat that starts and stops abruptly can be SVT. It is usually not dangerous but should be assessed; seek urgent care if you also have chest pain, faintness or breathlessness.
conditions.red: chest pain, fainting, or breathlessness with the fast heartbeat (seek emergency care)

conditions.name: Costochondritis (chest-wall inflammation)
conditions.action: Chest pain that is sharp, worse with movement or breathing, and tender when you press on the ribs, is often inflammation of the chest wall — not the heart. Anti-inflammatory pain relief helps. Still, get urgent help if pain is crushing, spreads to the arm/jaw, or comes with sweating or breathlessness.
conditions.red: crushing pain, pain spreading to arm/jaw, sweating or breathlessness (treat as possible heart attack)

conditions.name: Postural (orthostatic) low blood pressure
conditions.action: Feeling dizzy or faint when standing up can be a drop in blood pressure on standing — often from dehydration, medicines, or standing too quickly. Rise slowly, stay hydrated, and have medicines reviewed.
conditions.red: fainting with chest pain or palpitations, or black/tarry stools (possible bleed) — seek care

conditions.name: Outer ear infection (swimmer's ear)
conditions.action: Pain that is worse when you touch or pull the ear, often itchy and after swimming, is usually an outer-ear infection. Keep the ear dry; a clinician may prescribe ear drops.
conditions.red: spreading facial swelling, fever, or severe pain in someone with diabetes or weak immunity (seek urgent care)

conditions.name: Quinsy (peritonsillar abscess) — consider
conditions.action: A severe one-sided sore throat with a muffled voice, drooling, and trouble opening the mouth can be an abscess beside the tonsil. Seek same-day care; it usually needs draining and antibiotics.
conditions.red: difficulty breathing or swallowing your own saliva (emergency)

conditions.name: Tinnitus (ringing in the ears)
conditions.action: Ringing or buzzing in the ears is very common and usually not dangerous. A clinician can check your hearing and look for causes, especially if it is in one ear only or pulses with your heartbeat.
conditions.red: one-sided or pulsing tinnitus, sudden hearing loss, or dizziness (get checked)

conditions.name: Sudden hearing loss (consider)
conditions.action: Hearing that drops suddenly in one ear, without an obvious blockage, should be seen quickly — early treatment (often steroids) gives the best chance of recovery. See a clinician the same day.
conditions.red: hearing loss with weakness, slurred speech or a bad headache (seek emergency care)

conditions.name: Glue ear (otitis media with effusion, in children)
conditions.action: Dulled hearing in a child, often after colds or ear infections, can be fluid behind the eardrum ('glue ear'). It often clears on its own; a clinician can check and monitor hearing and speech.
conditions.red: a lot of ear pain with fever, or speech/development concerns

conditions.name: Hernia (groin or abdominal)
conditions.action: A soft bulge in the groin or tummy that appears on coughing, standing or lifting, and goes back when you lie down, is usually a hernia. Most are repaired when convenient — but if it becomes hard, very painful, red, or you start vomiting, that's an emergency (it may be trapped).
conditions.red: a hard, painful, red bulge with vomiting (trapped/strangulated — emergency)

conditions.name: Bowel obstruction — consider
conditions.action: A swollen, painful belly with vomiting and no bowel movement or wind can mean the bowel is blocked. Seek emergency care now — do not eat or drink.
conditions.red: severe pain, a rigid belly, or vomiting faeces-like fluid

conditions.name: Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's / colitis) — consider
conditions.action: Ongoing diarrhoea with blood or mucus, cramping, and weight loss over weeks can be inflammatory bowel disease. A GP can arrange tests and refer you to a gastroenterologist.
conditions.red: severe belly pain with a swollen rigid tummy and fever, or heavy rectal bleeding (seek urgent care)

conditions.name: Chronic kidney disease (assess)
conditions.action: Swollen ankles, frothy urine, itch and tiredness — especially with diabetes or high blood pressure — can reflect reduced kidney function. A GP can check this with simple blood and urine tests.
conditions.red: very little or no urine, severe breathlessness, or confusion (seek urgent care)

conditions.name: Epididymitis (testicle infection)
conditions.action: A gradually swelling, aching testicle — often with burning on passing urine — can be an infection (epididymitis). See a clinician the same day; it needs antibiotics. Sudden severe pain is different and an emergency (torsion).
conditions.red: sudden severe testicle pain, or nausea/vomiting (possible torsion — emergency)

conditions.name: Overactive bladder
conditions.action: A sudden, urgent need to pee — sometimes with leaking — without pain or infection, is often an overactive bladder. Bladder training, fluid/caffeine changes and sometimes medicines help a lot.
conditions.red: blood in the urine, pain, or fever (get checked for infection or other causes)

conditions.name: Scrotal swelling (hydrocele / varicocele)
conditions.action: A soft, usually painless scrotal swelling can be a fluid collection (hydrocele) or enlarged veins (varicocele). It should be examined, but is usually not dangerous. Sudden severe pain is an emergency.
conditions.red: sudden severe pain, a hard lump, or a swelling that doesn't go down lying flat (get checked)

conditions.name: Uterine fibroids (consider)
conditions.action: Heavy periods with pelvic pressure, bloating, or needing to pee often can be fibroids — common, benign growths in the womb. A gynaecologist can confirm and discuss options.
conditions.red: soaking through protection hourly, fainting, or severe sudden pelvic pain (seek urgent care)

conditions.name: Pelvic organ prolapse
conditions.action: A bulge or dragging feeling from the vagina is common, especially after childbirth or menopause, and is treatable. Pelvic-floor exercises help; a clinician can assess and offer pessaries or surgery.
conditions.red: being unable to pass urine, or a bulge that becomes painful or ulcerated (seek care)

conditions.name: Ovarian torsion — consider
conditions.action: Sudden, severe one-sided pelvic pain with nausea or vomiting can be a twisted ovary — a time-critical emergency. Seek emergency care now.
conditions.red: severe sudden pelvic pain with vomiting or faintness

conditions.name: Pre-eclampsia (consider)
conditions.action: In pregnancy (usually after 20 weeks), a bad headache, vision changes, upper-belly pain, or sudden swelling of the face and hands can signal pre-eclampsia — a dangerous rise in blood pressure. Seek emergency maternity care now.
conditions.red: severe headache, vision changes, upper-belly pain, or a fit

conditions.name: Gestational diabetes
conditions.action: High blood sugar found in pregnancy is usually managed well with diet, monitoring, and sometimes medicine, guided by your maternity team — this protects you and your baby.
conditions.red: very high sugars with vomiting, drowsiness or fruity breath (seek urgent care)

conditions.name: Psoriasis
conditions.action: Thick, scaly, silvery patches — often on elbows, knees or scalp — are typical of psoriasis, a long-term skin condition. A GP or dermatologist can confirm it and start treatment.
conditions.red: hot, widespread red skin with feeling unwell (rare severe flare — seek urgent care), or painful swollen joints

conditions.name: Rosacea
conditions.action: Persistent facial redness and flushing with small bumps, usually across the cheeks and nose, is often rosacea. Gentle skincare, avoiding triggers, and prescription creams/tablets help.
conditions.red: eye irritation and redness (ocular rosacea — get it checked)

conditions.name: Fungal nail infection
conditions.action: A thick, discoloured, crumbly nail is often a fungal infection. It's harmless but slow to treat; a clinician may confirm with a clipping before starting treatment.
conditions.red: spreading redness, pain and swelling around the nail with diabetes or poor circulation (get checked)

conditions.name: Warts / verrucas
conditions.action: Warts and verrucas are harmless skin growths from a common virus. Many clear on their own; over-the-counter treatments or a clinic can speed things up.
conditions.red: a growth that bleeds, changes, or won't heal (get it checked to be sure)

conditions.name: Hand, foot and mouth disease (children)
conditions.action: Blisters on the hands, feet and in the mouth with a mild fever, in a young child, is usually hand-foot-and-mouth — a common viral illness. It settles on its own; keep fluids up.
conditions.red: not drinking and fewer wet nappies, drowsiness, or a high fever that won't settle (seek care)

conditions.name: Cataracts
conditions.action: Slowly worsening cloudy or dim vision, glare, and faded colours are typical of cataracts, which are common with age. An optician/ophthalmologist can confirm it; surgery restores vision when it bothers you.
conditions.red: sudden vision loss, flashes/floaters, or a painful red eye (different problem — seek urgent eye care)

conditions.name: Macular degeneration (consider)
conditions.action: Blurring or distortion of your central vision (straight lines looking wavy, a central blur) can be macular degeneration. Get an eye assessment promptly — some types are treatable if caught early.
conditions.red: sudden central vision loss or rapidly worsening distortion (urgent eye care)

conditions.name: Stye (eyelid infection)
conditions.action: A painful red lump on the eyelid edge is usually a stye. Warm compresses several times a day help it settle; most clear on their own.
conditions.red: spreading redness/swelling of the whole lid or face, or vision change (seek urgent care)

conditions.name: Corneal abrasion (scratched eye)
conditions.action: A scratched, painful, watering eye with the feeling of something in it is often a corneal abrasion. Don't rub it; get it checked the same day — it usually heals quickly with eye drops.
conditions.red: a chemical splash, a high-speed injury, or marked vision loss (emergency eye care now)

conditions.name: Burst blood vessel on the eye
conditions.action: A bright red, painless patch on the white of the eye is usually a harmless burst blood vessel that clears on its own. Get it checked if it was from an injury, or if there's pain or vision change.
conditions.red: an injury, pain, vision change, or you take blood thinners (get checked)

conditions.name: Bursitis
conditions.action: A tender, swollen area over a joint (often the knee or elbow) from kneeling, leaning or overuse is usually bursitis. Rest, ice, and anti-inflammatory pain relief help.
conditions.red: hot, very painful, red swelling with fever (possible infection — seek urgent care)

conditions.name: Frozen shoulder
conditions.action: A shoulder that is stiff and painful and won't lift, over weeks to months, can be a frozen shoulder. Physiotherapy and pain relief help; it slowly improves.
conditions.red: shoulder weakness/numbness after an injury, or unable to move it at all after trauma (get checked)

conditions.name: Ankylosing spondylitis (consider)
conditions.action: Back stiffness that is worse in the morning and eases with movement, lasting months in a younger adult, can be an inflammatory arthritis of the spine. A GP can arrange tests and refer to rheumatology.
conditions.red: new leg weakness, numbness, or bladder/bowel changes (seek urgent care)

conditions.name: Osteoporosis (thin bones) — consider
conditions.action: Breaking a bone from a minor fall, or losing height with a rounded upper back, can point to thinning bones (osteoporosis). A GP can arrange a bone-density scan and treatment to reduce future fractures.
conditions.red: sudden severe back pain after a minor strain in an older adult (possible spinal fracture — get seen)

conditions.name: Tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis)
conditions.action: Pain on the outside of the elbow when gripping or lifting is usually tennis elbow, an overuse strain of the tendon. Rest, load changes, and physiotherapy help; it settles with time.
conditions.red: numbness/tingling into the hand, or pain after a fall (get checked)

conditions.name: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (consider)
conditions.action: Unwanted intrusive thoughts with rituals or repeated checking that you can't stop, and that take up time or cause distress, can be OCD. It is very treatable — a GP can refer you for therapy.
conditions.red: thoughts of harming yourself or others (reach out for urgent support)

conditions.name: Postnatal depression (consider)
conditions.action: Feeling persistently low, hopeless, tearful or unable to bond in the weeks and months after having a baby can be postnatal depression. It is common and treatable — please reach out to your GP, midwife or health visitor.
conditions.red: thoughts of harming yourself or the baby, or feeling unable to cope (seek urgent help now)

conditions.name: Chickenpox
conditions.action: Crops of itchy spots that turn into blisters then scabs, with a mild fever, are typical of chickenpox. It settles on its own; keep comfortable and avoid scratching. Stay away from pregnant people, newborns and anyone with weak immunity.
conditions.red: breathing trouble, drowsiness, a very high fever, or blisters that become hot, spreading and painful (seek urgent care)

conditions.name: Mumps (consider)
conditions.action: Painful swelling of the cheeks and jaw (the salivary glands) with fever can be mumps, especially if unvaccinated. See a clinician; it is usually self-limiting but can have complications.
conditions.red: severe headache with a stiff neck, severe belly pain, or testicle pain/swelling (seek urgent care)

conditions.name: Swallowed a chemical / corrosive
conditions.action: Swallowing bleach, cleaners, antifreeze or similar is an emergency. Do NOT make them vomit. Call your local emergency number and Poison Control now with the product name. In the US and Canada call Poison Control 1-800-222-1222; elsewhere call your local poison centre or emergency number.
conditions.red: drooling, mouth burns, trouble breathing or swallowing, or drowsiness

conditions.name: Swallowed a poison (consider)
conditions.action: If someone has swallowed a poison (rat poison, weedkiller, unknown berries) or you think they've been poisoned, call your local emergency number and Poison Control now with the product name or a photo. Do not make them vomit unless told to. In the US and Canada call Poison Control 1-800-222-1222; elsewhere call your local poison centre or emergency number.
conditions.red: drowsiness, trouble breathing, fits, or vomiting blood

conditions.name: Alcohol poisoning
conditions.action: Someone who can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, is cold/clammy, or keeps vomiting after heavy drinking may have alcohol poisoning. Call your local emergency number now. Keep them on their side (recovery position), don't leave them alone, and don't give coffee or try to walk it off.
conditions.red: slow/irregular breathing, blue lips, cold skin, fits, or can't be woken

conditions.name: Knocked-out or broken tooth
conditions.action: A knocked-out adult tooth is a dental emergency — handle it by the crown (not the root), gently rinse, and if you can, place it back in the socket or keep it in milk (or saliva), then see a dentist within an hour. A chipped tooth or lost filling needs a routine dental visit.
conditions.red: facial swelling with fever, or trouble breathing/swallowing (seek urgent care)

conditions.name: Limping or non-using limb in a child
conditions.action: A child who is limping or won't use an arm or leg should be checked the same day — causes range from minor injury to an infection or fracture. A hot, swollen, painful joint with fever is an emergency.
conditions.red: a hot swollen joint with fever, severe pain, or being unwell (seek emergency care)

conditions.name: Eye pain on movement / bulging eye — consider
conditions.action: Pain when moving the eye, or a bulging, very swollen eye, needs urgent eye assessment — it can mean inflammation of the optic nerve or an infection behind the eye (orbital cellulitis). Seek same-day eye care.
conditions.red: vision loss, double vision, fever, or inability to move the eye (emergency)

conditions.name: Very slow heartbeat — consider
conditions.action: A very slow heartbeat (for example in the 30s–40s) with dizziness, faintness, breathlessness or chest pain needs same-day assessment. Call your local emergency number if you faint, have chest pain, or feel very unwell.
conditions.red: fainting, chest pain, or severe breathlessness with the slow pulse (emergency)

conditions.name: Chemical burn to the skin or eye
conditions.action: Rinse the area with plenty of running water for at least 20 minutes, remove contaminated clothing/jewellery, and don't rub. For the eye, keep rinsing and get emergency eye care. Call your local emergency number or Poison Control with the product name.
conditions.red: a chemical in the eye, a large/deep burn, or trouble breathing from fumes

conditions.name: Electric shock injury
conditions.action: After an electric shock, make sure the power is off before touching the person. Even if they seem fine, a significant shock (high voltage, a shock across the body, or any loss of consciousness) needs emergency assessment — the heart rhythm and hidden burns can be affected. Call your local emergency number.
conditions.red: collapse, palpitations, burns, or loss of consciousness

conditions.name: Near-drowning / inhaled water
conditions.action: Anyone who nearly drowned should be assessed, even if they seem okay — breathing problems can develop over the next several hours from inhaled water. Call your local emergency number if there is any cough, breathlessness, or drowsiness.
conditions.red: breathing trouble, a persistent cough, drowsiness, or blue lips

conditions.name: Very high blood sugar (consider)
conditions.action: A very high blood sugar should be acted on. Follow your diabetes sick-day plan, check for ketones if you can, and drink water. Seek emergency care now if you have deep fast breathing, fruity breath, vomiting, drowsiness or belly pain (possible diabetic ketoacidosis).
conditions.red: vomiting, deep/fast breathing, fruity breath, drowsiness, or belly pain (DKA — emergency)

conditions.name: Low oxygen level — consider
conditions.action: A low oxygen reading (for example in the 80s) with breathlessness needs urgent assessment. Call your local emergency number, especially if you are struggling to breathe, your lips look blue, or you feel very unwell. (A cold hand or poor probe fit can give a falsely low reading — recheck if you feel well.)
conditions.red: blue lips, severe breathlessness, confusion or drowsiness

conditions.name: Missed dialysis
conditions.action: Missing dialysis can cause a dangerous build-up of fluid and potassium. Contact your renal unit now. Seek emergency care if you are breathless, have chest pain, palpitations, or severe weakness.
conditions.red: breathlessness, chest pain, palpitations, or muscle weakness

conditions.name: Priapism (prolonged painful erection)
conditions.action: A painful erection lasting more than a few hours is an emergency — go to the emergency department now. Delayed treatment can cause permanent damage. While waiting, it may help to pass urine, walk, or apply a cold pack.
conditions.red: an erection lasting over 4 hours, or severe pain

conditions.name: Paraphimosis (trapped foreskin)
conditions.action: A foreskin that is stuck behind the head of the penis and swelling is an emergency — it can cut off blood supply. Go to emergency care now; firm steady squeezing of the swelling can sometimes reduce it while you get help.
conditions.red: increasing swelling, severe pain, or the tip turning dusky/blue

conditions.name: Newborn cord infection (omphalitis) — consider
conditions.action: Redness spreading around a newborn's belly button, with smell, discharge, or the baby being unwell, can be a serious infection. Babies get sick fast — seek emergency care now.
conditions.red: spreading redness, fever, poor feeding, or a floppy/drowsy baby

conditions.name: Gangrene / dead tissue — consider
conditions.action: Skin or a toe/finger turning black or looking dead can mean the tissue has lost its blood supply or is severely infected. This is an emergency, especially with diabetes or poor circulation — go now.
conditions.red: spreading blackness, severe pain, fever, or feeling very unwell

conditions.name: Fainting on exertion — consider
conditions.action: Fainting or nearly fainting during exercise or exertion can point to a heart problem and should be assessed promptly — stop strenuous activity until you've been checked. Seek emergency care if it comes with chest pain or palpitations.
conditions.red: fainting with chest pain, palpitations, or a family history of sudden death (urgent)

conditions.name: Gambling disorder (support)
conditions.action: Gambling that you can't control and that harms your life, money or relationships is a recognised health problem — and help works. A GP or a gambling support service can help confidentially, at your pace.
conditions.red: thoughts of harming yourself (reach out for urgent support)

conditions.name: Tuberculosis (TB) — consider
conditions.action: TB is a lung infection spread through the air when an infected person coughs. A cough lasting over three weeks with night sweats, weight loss, or coughing up blood needs testing soon. TB is curable with a course of antibiotics, and testing and treatment are usually free and confidential — contact a doctor or TB/public-health clinic.
conditions.red: coughing up blood, breathlessness, or severe weight loss (seek care urgently)

conditions.name: RSV / bronchiolitis in a baby — consider
conditions.action: RSV is a common winter virus that can cause wheezy, laboured breathing in babies (bronchiolitis). It spreads by coughs, sneezes and hands. Most babies recover at home, but seek urgent care if the baby breathes fast, sucks in under the ribs, goes blue, is too breathless to feed, or has long pauses in breathing.
conditions.red: fast or laboured breathing, blueness, poor feeding, or pauses in breathing (emergency)

conditions.name: Norovirus (stomach bug)
conditions.action: Norovirus is a very contagious stomach bug spreading by hands, surfaces and food. It causes sudden vomiting and diarrhoea that usually settles in 1-3 days. The main risk is dehydration — sip fluids often. Wash hands with soap (hand gel works poorly against it), and stay off work/school until 48 hours after symptoms stop.
conditions.red: signs of dehydration, blood in stool, or no improvement after a few days (seek care)

conditions.name: Head lice
conditions.action: Head lice are small insects that live in hair and spread by head-to-head contact. They are harmless but itchy. Treat with wet-combing with conditioner or a pharmacy lotion, and check close contacts. There is no need to keep children off school.
conditions.red: spreading redness, pus, or a sore infected scalp from scratching (see a pharmacist or doctor)

conditions.name: Malaria — consider (after travel)
conditions.action: Malaria is a serious infection from mosquito bites in affected regions, and it can become life-threatening within days. Any fever within a year of travel to a malaria area — but especially the first 3 months — is an emergency. Go to emergency care now and tell them where and when you travelled.
conditions.red: confusion, drowsiness, fits, breathlessness, or very little urine (severe malaria — emergency)

conditions.name: Dengue — consider (after travel)
conditions.action: Dengue is a mosquito-borne virus in tropical regions causing high fever, severe aches and a rash. Most recover, but warning signs around days 3-7 (as the fever drops) can mean a dangerous phase. Seek care for any fever after tropical travel, and go urgently for belly pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding, or extreme tiredness. Avoid ibuprofen/aspirin — use paracetamol.
conditions.red: severe belly pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding gums/nose, or a cold, clammy state (emergency)

conditions.name: Typhoid — consider (after travel)
conditions.action: Typhoid is a bacterial infection from contaminated food or water in some regions, causing a rising sustained fever, headache and tummy upset. It needs antibiotics. Seek care promptly for a sustained fever after travel, and say where you went.
conditions.red: severe abdominal pain, confusion, or bleeding (seek urgent care)

conditions.name: Rubella (German measles) — consider
conditions.action: Rubella is a viral infection with a mild rash and swollen glands, spread by coughs and sneezes. It is usually mild — BUT it can seriously harm an unborn baby. If you are or could be pregnant, phone your doctor first rather than attending in person. Stay away from pregnant people until cleared.
conditions.red: pregnancy, or a pregnant contact (contact a doctor without delay)

conditions.name: Male/female pattern hair loss (androgenetic alopecia)
conditions.action: Pattern hair loss is the common, gradual thinning with age — a receding hairline and thinning crown in men, and widening parting in women. It is not dangerous. If it bothers you, a pharmacist or GP can discuss options such as topical minoxidil; a doctor can check for other causes (thyroid, iron, medicines) if loss is rapid or patchy.
conditions.red: sudden patchy loss, scarring, or loss with other symptoms (see a doctor)

conditions.name: Alopecia areata (patchy hair loss) — consider
conditions.action: Alopecia areata causes sudden, smooth round bald patches when the immune system targets hair follicles. It is not contagious and hair often regrows. A GP or dermatologist can confirm it and discuss treatment, and check for linked conditions like thyroid problems.
conditions.red: rapidly spreading loss or loss of all scalp/body hair (see a doctor)

conditions.name: Hair shedding after stress/illness (telogen effluvium)
conditions.action: Heavy, diffuse hair shedding a few months after a trigger — illness, high fever, childbirth, surgery, major stress or a crash diet — is usually telogen effluvium. It is temporary and the hair regrows once the trigger passes. A GP can check iron, thyroid and medicines if it drags on beyond 6 months.
conditions.red: shedding lasting over 6 months, or with other symptoms (see a doctor)

conditions.name: Sleep disorder (non-apnoea) — consider
conditions.action: Acting out dreams, falling asleep suddenly in the day, teeth-grinding or sleepwalking can point to a treatable sleep disorder. A GP can assess and may refer to a sleep clinic; teeth-grinding is also worth a dentist's review for a night guard. Falling asleep uncontrollably by day affects driving safety — mention it.
conditions.red: falling asleep while driving, or acting out dreams with injury (see a doctor promptly)

conditions.name: Alcohol use — support
conditions.action: Drinking that you can't control, or that's harming your health, mood, work or relationships, is common and treatable — and help is confidential. A GP or an alcohol support service can help you cut down safely (stopping suddenly after heavy daily drinking can be dangerous, so get advice first).
conditions.red: shakes, sweats, confusion or seizures when you stop drinking (seek medical help — withdrawal can be dangerous)

conditions.name: Breastfeeding support
conditions.action: Latch and supply worries are very common and usually fixable with the right support. A midwife, health visitor, or a breastfeeding/lactation specialist can watch a feed and help. Seek same-day care if the baby has fewer wet nappies, is very sleepy or not waking to feed, or you have a hot painful breast with fever (possible mastitis).
conditions.red: a hot painful breast with fever, or a baby with few wet nappies or too sleepy to feed (seek care)

conditions.name: Postnatal wound infection — consider
conditions.action: Stitches or a caesarean wound that are increasingly red, hot, swollen, smelly or leaking after birth may be infected and need prompt treatment. Contact your midwife or doctor the same day. Go urgently with fever, feeling very unwell, or heavy bleeding.
conditions.red: fever, spreading redness, heavy bleeding, or feeling very unwell (seek urgent care)

conditions.name: Overdue pregnancy (post-dates)
conditions.action: Going past your due date is common. Your midwife will monitor you and usually offer a membrane sweep and discuss induction, typically by around 41-42 weeks. Contact your midwife to arrange checks, and seek urgent care if the baby's movements reduce, your waters break, or you have bleeding.
conditions.red: reduced fetal movements, bleeding, or waters breaking (contact maternity urgently)

conditions.name: Common benign skin lump or mark — likely
conditions.action: Skin tags, soft moveable lumps (lipomas), age spots and patches of lighter or darker skin are usually harmless. No treatment is needed unless they bother you. See a GP or pharmacist to confirm, and — importantly — get any spot checked that is changing, growing, bleeding, crusting, or won't heal, as those features need a proper skin check.
conditions.red: a lesion that changes, grows, bleeds, itches, or won't heal (get it checked)

conditions.name: Child development concern
conditions.action: Worries about a child's speech, social interaction, movement or head shape are worth raising early — support works best when started young. See your GP, health visitor, or paediatric service for a developmental review; a flat head (positional) is common and usually improves with repositioning. Trust your instincts and ask for an assessment.
conditions.red: loss of skills already gained, or a child who is floppy, not feeding, or very unwell (seek prompt care)

conditions.name: Bedwetting (nocturnal enuresis)
conditions.action: Bedwetting is common and not the child's fault; it often improves with time and simple measures. See your GP if it continues past about age 5-7, is new after being dry, or comes with daytime wetting, pain passing urine, or excessive thirst — those need checking. Support (fluids timing, bedwetting alarm, sometimes medication) helps.
conditions.red: new bedwetting after being dry, daytime wetting, pain passing urine, or excessive thirst (get checked)

conditions.name: Blocked urinary catheter — consider
conditions.action: A catheter that stops draining can let the bladder fill painfully and can cause harm, especially with belly pain, feeling unwell, or (in spinal-injury patients) sweating and high blood pressure. Contact the district/community nurse or go to urgent care. Do not leave it blocked.
conditions.red: lower-belly pain or swelling, no urine for hours, fever, or feeling very unwell (urgent)

conditions.name: Workplace/occupational exposure — consider
conditions.action: Feeling unwell that may be linked to a workplace hazard (lead, solvents, fumes, dust) is worth checking — tell your GP exactly what you work with, as specific blood or other tests and reporting may apply. Seek urgent care for breathing difficulty, collapse, or severe symptoms. Report hazards to your workplace health and safety.
conditions.red: breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse, or severe symptoms (urgent care)

conditions.name: Contraception check (coil/pill)
conditions.action: Changes in your coil (IUD) threads, or questions about contraception, are worth a check with your GP or a sexual-health/family-planning clinic. Use extra protection (condoms) until it's confirmed in place. Seek prompt care for severe pelvic pain, fever, or heavy bleeding, or if pregnancy is possible with pain.
conditions.red: severe pelvic pain, fever, heavy bleeding, or a positive pregnancy test with pain (seek prompt care)

conditions.name: Acute urinary retention — consider
conditions.action: Suddenly being unable to pass any urine while the bladder fills and hurts is acute urinary retention — it needs prompt draining with a catheter. Go to urgent/emergency care the same day. Treat it as an emergency if it comes with new numbness between the legs, back pain, or loss of bowel control (possible cauda equina).
conditions.red: back pain with groin/saddle numbness or loss of bowel control (emergency — possible cauda equina)

conditions.name: Black tarry stools (possible upper GI bleed) — consider
conditions.action: Black, tarry, sticky stools (melena) usually mean partly-digested blood from higher in the gut (stomach or small bowel) — for example a bleeding ulcer. This needs urgent assessment. Go to urgent/emergency care, and treat it as an emergency if you feel faint, dizzy, very pale, or are also vomiting blood. (Iron tablets and some foods can also darken stool, but it is safer to get checked.)
conditions.red: feeling faint, dizzy, very pale, vomiting blood, or a fast heartbeat (emergency)

conditions.name: Bulging fontanelle in a baby — consider
conditions.action: A bulging, tense soft spot (fontanelle) on a baby — especially with fever, vomiting, drowsiness, a high-pitched cry, or a non-fading rash — can mean raised pressure in the skull or meningitis. This is an emergency: go to emergency care now.
conditions.red: fever, drowsiness, vomiting, a high-pitched cry, fits, or a rash that doesn't fade (emergency)

conditions.name: Lump, boil or ingrown hair near the anus/tailbone — consider
conditions.action: A painful lump, boil or ingrown hair around the anus or tailbone is usually an infected hair follicle (folliculitis or a boil), a perianal abscess, or a pilonidal cyst/sinus at the top of the buttocks. Many settle with warm salt-water soaks and good hygiene, but a growing, very painful or pus-filled lump often needs a clinician to drain it and sometimes antibiotics. Book to be seen in the next day or two.
conditions.red: spreading redness, fever or feeling unwell, fast-growing or severe pain, or you have diabetes or a weak immune system — be seen urgently
